cutoverUnits.description: Request timing, protected context, headers, rules, classification, deduplication, and resource-state handoff.
Document-start Worker, fetch, XHR, JSON, TextDecoder, key, manifest, and page-action runtime bundle.
MediaSource capture, bounded page buffering, main spool, reset, finalize, and merge lifecycle.
HLS parse, plan, key, map, range, rendition, live, retry, preprocessing, and byte-output semantics.
DASH parse, plan, BaseURL, timeline, track, range, download, merge, and rejection semantics.
Concurrent transfer, Range, retry, abort, ordered output, cancellation, memory budget, and task ownership.
Verified staged output, leases, ffmpeg, local save, library delivery, normal downloads, external tools, and workflow projection.

capabilities.notes: The unregistered Electron adapter now preserves Cat Catch request-stage regex handling and response-start classification, binds each redirect hop to a fresh onSendHeaders event, cleans pending state on redirect/completion/error/dispose, rejects stale navigation owners, and converts vault invalidation into revisioned Store changes. The legacy onCompleted bridge remains the only production owner until the network-capture unit cutover.

acceptedDifferences: When Cat Catch regex classification rewrites a request URL, OmniFlow does not inherit credentials from the observed URL; a new main-owned context is required for the rewritten exact URL.

After an HTTP redirect, OmniFlow never forwards the previous hop's protected headers, including for a same-origin target. The target needs its own main-owned captured context; page-drag staging may still use the captured tab's Electron session cookie jar for cookies scoped to the target URL.
capabilities.notes: The pinned main-only vault preserves Cat Catch's protected-header selection and adds bounded pending/retained lifecycles, opaque renderer-safe projection, purpose and owner bindings, independent source/replay resource types, exact resource URL redemption, page-drag Cookie policy, and value-free invalidation events for every retained context deletion reason. The unregistered CapturedResourceAccessService now accepts only tabId, opaque resourceId, and one of four fixed purposes; it derives URL, replay type, owner generation, page origin, WebContents, and header values from Store/Vault, rejects stale owners for both context-bearing and context-free resources, forces manual redirect, and strips protected headers from every later hop. Page-drag omits the captured Cookie and requests cookie-jar credentials through a mandatory injected transport; production captured-source wiring now binds that transport to the captured tab's Electron session, while unrecognized/data/blob fallback remains in the legacy staging service. Download, inspection, captured-source page-drag, and external-tool consumers now have the target authority; inspection has a main-owned byte budget and safe result projection, and download/page-drag pass the authorized Response only to an injected main sink and never accept renderer URL/header/redirect/destination fields. Full production cutover and cleanup remain open.

Pinned pure port covers full-string case-insensitive wildcard page rules, disabled-rule skipping, the default-off Douyin forced block, blacklist/whitelist inversion, and special-page protocol checks. It does not own per-tab membership and is not connected to production. The current local domain rules filter resource hosts rather than Cat Catch's top-level page/tab URL, so a later adapter must map that product difference explicitly.

capabilities.notes: Pinned pure port covers ordered request regex, upstream default rule states, extension/MIME/Content-Disposition/media fallback precedence, hard break semantics, size operators, wildcard MIME priority, and exact-URL dedupe/reset decisions. A separate OmniFlow capture policy now adds image, key, document, and expanded-subtitle kinds at the target adapter boundary: Cat Catch capture results remain authoritative, regex blacklist is never overridden, and non-product media rejection remains intact. The persisted OmniFlow extension, MIME, regex, domain whitelist, and domain blacklist settings compile into this target policy, and the unregistered runtime can replace the compiled settings without replacing its owned webRequest listeners. Production still uses the legacy classifier/rules until atomic cutover.

acceptedDifferences: OmniFlow expires captured resource metadata after six hours and releases main-only request contexts on capacity reset, TTL sweep, navigation clear, tab/WebContents disposal, and application disposal; Cat Catch has no equivalent resource TTL or main-only context lifecycle.

OmniFlow stable probe resources upsert by navigation generation plus page-owned resource key. Updating an existing key keeps its opaque id even at capacity, while the same key in a later document creates a new resource instead of merging metadata across pages.

Renderer-safe state exposes opaque resource ids, revision/incarnation stamps, and whitelisted metadata/header capabilities only; page resource keys, context refs and values, page origin, WebContents id, and captured navigation owner facts remain main-owned.
capabilities.notes: The pinned main-only store preserves the desktop 10,000-entry overflow reset/drop behavior, exact-URL dedupe including the 500-fingerprint reset boundary, explicit navigation clear/retain, stable probe upsert, bounded TTL, newest-first snapshots, single-owner context release, and revision/incarnation tombstones. The unregistered PageProbeCaptureAdapter binds one document generation to deep-only stable-key writes, ignores page-supplied tab/timestamp authority, keeps resourceKey main-only, and emits every accepted upsert through the same revisioned change path. EmbeddedBrowserCaptureRuntime resolves an opaque probe resource id back to its page key only while the tab, incarnation, navigation generation, page origin and WebContents owner all remain current; renderer never receives that key. The target composition is not connected to the production console listener yet. NetworkContextVault invalidations already feed Store changes through the target network adapter; the legacy Map remains the only production owner until atomic cutover.

The target contract now owns renderer-safe resource/snapshot/change DTOs, whitelist parsing, and the revision/incarnation reducer. The new Store imports and re-exports these types for migration compatibility. Legacy preload, ambient, and renderer DTO copies remain reachable only through the production legacy chain and must be removed in the atomic network-capture cutover.

The unregistered target lifecycle and EmbeddedBrowserCaptureRuntime compose exactly one network adapter, the context vault, resource store, safe change contract, per-view tokenized probe adapter, opaque access authority, and bounded inspection through fake Electron integration. The runtime owns tab/view registration and replacement, explicit clear/retain navigation, crash quarantine and recovery, spontaneous WebContents destruction, explicit tab/WebContents close, closeAll, maintenance, and application disposal; constructing it claims the session webRequest listener boundary, so production must not instantiate it before the atomic cutover. Probe ingress is minted only while capture mode is deep. ElectronPageProbeEventAdapter owns separate current-document and pre-signed next-navigation routes: the next document-start token is promoted only after its expected incarnation/navigation binding becomes current, while the previous token remains invalid. Every message rechecks the binding and current deep mode; malformed/base-prefix/old-token/crashed/disposed/stopped messages are ignored, only mse-flush/mse-reset reach the separate control callback, and callback errors are contained. Ordinary discovery payloads without a page key receive a main-derived stable key that remains opaque. Production controller/view lifecycle still uses the legacy recorder until protected-context consumers, IPC/preload/renderer projection, production probe installation, and atomic cutover are ready.
Known seed gap: enableDeepRuntimeHooks is hard-coded false; Worker/fetch/XHR/JSON/key hooks are inactive, TextDecoder is absent, and JSON limits differ from upstream.
Current heuristics exist but no complete upstream behavior map or differential test coverage is recorded.
Seed security gap: the console-prefix envelope has no nonce or capability validation, so an untrusted page can forge resource and MSE events.
The eight current toolkit preferences are persisted in each visited site's origin localStorage, not in an application-level owner; capture enabled state itself is memory-only.
MSE is the only currently active runtime hook family; parity, bounded page retention, and append/endOfStream observability are unverified.
Spool files and write queues are controller Maps with no global budget, reaper, quarantine, crash recovery, or app-exit cleanup.

acceptedDifferences: Pinned hls.js records the first variable parsing error on the playlist and its evented loader rejects that parse; the synchronous OmniFlow facade throws the same first error because it has no loader event boundary.

Pinned hls.js emits levelEmptyError after manifest loading when a media playlist has no complete fragment; the synchronous OmniFlow facade throws the same No Segments found in Playlist error before creating a download plan.
Pinned hls.js reports malformed media playlists through levelParsingError before LEVEL_LOADED; the synchronous OmniFlow facade throws the same parsing reason before creating a download plan.

Pinned hls.js may reject an all-unknown-codec master later against browser MediaSource support; the OmniFlow pure parser preserves those normal variants for its ffmpeg execution boundary and does not make renderer codec support an execution authority.
capabilities.notes: The pure Cat Catch parser now owns the manifest parse path behind the renderer compatibility facade, resolves an omitted media BYTERANGE offset from the immediately previous fragment even when the URI changes, resets each EXT-X-MAP range with an omitted offset to zero, preserves the initial discontinuity sequence, and materializes AES-128 effective IVs from each media sequence or sequence zero for an encrypted EXT-X-MAP. Each map captures the key context active at its declaration independently from the later media key, matching hls.js BaseSegment.setByteRange, setInitSegment, LevelKey.getDecryptData, and parseLevelPlaylist. LL-HLS EXT-X-PART entries remain outside the downloadable fragment list because pinned hls.js stores them in LevelDetails.partList while Cat Catch parseTs copies only LevelDetails.fragments; complete EXTINF sequence and duration therefore stay authoritative, and empty or PART-only media playlists are rejected before plan creation with the pinned loader error. Master parsing now exposes only normal EXT-X-STREAM-INF levels, rejects a master with no normal levels, and removes mixed-in unknown codec levels whenever at least one level has only the vendored hls.js 1.6.16 known codec prefixes; I-frame streams no longer enter Cat Catch's selectable data.levels. Media playlists also preserve the pinned structural rejection boundary for a missing EXTM3U delimiter or target duration, repeated TARGETDURATION/PLAYLIST-TYPE, and MEDIA-SEQUENCE/DISCONTINUITY-SEQUENCE tags placed after the first fragment, so malformed input cannot become an executable plan. EXT-X-DEFINE now follows pinned hls.js 1.6.16 for NAME/VALUE, QUERYPARAM, explicit master-to-media IMPORT, single-pass variable replacement in URI lines plus quoted/hexadecimal attributes, and first-error duplicate/missing rejection. The renderer compatibility facade carries the master variable list into its explicit local child-playlist resolver; live recording derives the same list from the main-owned captured master only when a child declares IMPORT, validates that the selected child belongs to that master, and never accepts renderer-supplied variable values. The broader upstream parser/dependency behavior remains unverified. Vendor provenance blocker: the bundled jQuery banner reports 4.0.0 while lib/third-party-libraries.md declares 3.7.1.

acceptedDifferences: Cat Catch decrypts AES-128 fragments in its JavaScript downloader; OmniFlow preserves the pure key/IV behavior port but delegates production local-playlist decryption and remuxing to the single cancellable ffmpeg owner, avoiding a second decrypt pass.
capabilities.notes: Plan execution now accepts a main-owned fetch transport: captured fragment/key/map URLs are redeemed through the current tab resource authority with bounded Range support, while unrecognized URLs retain the embedded-session fallback. Direct HLS download now accepts only one exact opaque resource id; track merge accepts independent video/audio resource ids, redeems each URL and protected header set in main, and applies the two header sets to separate ffmpeg inputs. Renderer resolves those ids only from the current active resource snapshot and explicitly rejects uncaptured selected child manifests instead of reusing a parent authority. The fragment downloader now supports an ordered async processor chain, emits each processed stage, retries failed fetch or processor attempts, and exposes an aborted terminal event. HLS local execution carries one AbortSignal through key, map, and media-fragment fetches and destroys the downloader on success, failure, or cancellation, preserving the Cat Catch use() pipeline boundary for decrypt/transcode steps. Its rewritten playlist deduplicates fetched key bytes by method and URL but tracks METHOD, local URI, IV, and KEYFORMAT as playlist state, so sequence-derived or explicit IV rotation re-emits EXT-X-KEY without redownloading identical key bytes. Encrypted init data keeps the map's declaration-time key separate from the media key and rewrites in playback order as map-key -> EXT-X-MAP -> media-key -> EXTINF; identical key or map bytes remain resource-deduplicated. A production-contract smoke verifies the rewritten local playlist plus key/map/media files are handed to the ffmpeg wrapper and that zero-exit without a non-empty output is rejected; conditional real-binary integrations verify clear HLS plus AES-128 encrypted local HLS with both explicit and nonzero-sequence implicit IV through the production ffmpeg wrapper, then use ffprobe to prove non-empty MP4 output with an AAC stream and positive duration. The tab/request-scoped HLS session owner now holds active direct/track/plan/retry/live-export tasks, retry/live state, and at most 32 latest safe task projections. Every emitted projection receives a main-owned monotonic revision; renderer subscribes before reading the snapshot IPC, rejects older revisions and restores only the current tab plus current manifest/variant/rendition set. Ordinary task projections survive renderer listener remount; live recording still discards on tool unmount and cleans its frozen output directory because the library delivery target is not application-scoped yet. Production navigation, tab close, view destruction, render-process loss, controller disposal, and application graceful shutdown all route through one HLS host lifecycle; it aborts and awaits active work, clears task projections, removes retry/live work directories, and controller disposal also waits for cleanup already claimed by an earlier lifecycle event. Vendor provenance blockers: lib/third-party-libraries.md attributes m3u8-decrypt.js to the mutable hls.js master path rather than an immutable revision; the loaded StreamSaver bundle self-reports 2.0.5 while that document declares 2.0.6, has no verified immutable artifact binding, and retains remote MITM configuration.

Live start accepts an opaque resourceId and binds captured manifest/segment polling to the current tab's authority-aware fetch; unrecognized URLs still use the embedded-session fallback. When a selected child playlist declares EXT-X-DEFINE:IMPORT, the recorder lazily asks a main-owned resolver to fetch the original captured master with its retained authority, verifies that the child URL belongs to that master, and reuses only the explicitly imported variable list across later polls; the resolver shares the recorder AbortSignal and renderer values cannot override it. Its initial manifest request preserves Cat Catch's single force-cache recovery after an HTTP failure; later live polls and response-less network errors do not retry. The recorder owns one AbortController across parent resolution, manifest and segment polling, exposes discard, and has executable terminal/discard tests. Consecutive LL-HLS snapshots append only newly completed EXTINF fragments; partial and preload entries neither download nor inflate cumulative duration. Main keeps a bounded live task projection, but the feature-scoped library delivery target cannot be reconstructed after unmount yet; switching HLS request or unmounting the tool therefore discards the live session and cleans the frozen output directory instead of presenting a false recovery. A newly mounted renderer does not adopt a briefly retained live snapshot while that discard is settling. Navigation, tab close, view destruction, render-process loss, controller disposal, and graceful application exit route through the production HLS host lifecycle; live export ffmpeg is registered as an active task, so cleanup aborts and awaits it before discarding the recorder, task projection, and work directory. Concurrent lifecycle cleanup is tracked so shutdown cannot finish while an earlier discard/workdir cleanup is still pending. Vendor provenance blocker: the upstream live path depends on the same unverified StreamSaver 2.0.5/2.0.6 bundle and remote MITM configuration recorded by transfer.streaming-memory-budget.

The pure port preserves Cat Catch's conservative PNG/JPEG prefix removal with an unchanged-buffer fallback for incomplete signatures. The local HLS fragment downloader applies it after rawBuffer emission and before sequential output in current local-plan and live-recording paths, with decrypt/preprocess ordering covered independently. Captured HLS inspection and the initial live manifest request now make exactly one same-URL force-cache attempt after a non-success HTTP response, retain main-owned authority headers, never retry response-less network errors, and do not apply the branch to MPD or later live polls. Fake and real-binary output integrations cover the downstream handoff; website-level manual validation remains open.

The current hand-written renderer parser is not supported by a mature parser oracle or complete specification fixtures. Vendor provenance blockers: the bundled mpd-parser banner reports 1.4.0 while lib/third-party-libraries.md declares 1.4.1, and the bundled jQuery banner reports 4.0.0 while that document declares 3.7.1.

Known seed gap includes SegmentTimeline r=-1 and incomplete dynamic MPD semantics; plan segment/init requests now accept a main-owned fetch transport for captured URLs, while the renderer-supplied plan shape and unrecognized URL fallback remain transitional.

Local AbortControllers exist inside the downloader, but the orchestration layer does not retain a uniform cancel handle or terminal task record. Vendor provenance blockers: the bundled jQuery banner reports 4.0.0 while lib/third-party-libraries.md declares 3.7.1; the loaded StreamSaver bundle has the unresolved provenance recorded by transfer.streaming-memory-budget.

Pinned upstream defaults catDownload=false, so eligible native download failures enter the Cat Catch downloader; true disables that fallback. The same session shell reuses or creates a downloader tab and closes it after stream, ffmpeg, or browser-download terminal events while guarding unload. OmniFlow currently splits native download events and fragment execution across owners and has no equivalent fallback/session coordinator.

Known gap: direct downloads and selected HTTP/resource reads materialize complete responses in memory. Vendor provenance blocker: the vendored StreamSaver bundle has no verified immutable upstream artifact binding, self-reports 2.0.5 while lib/third-party-libraries.md declares 2.0.6, and retains remote MITM bindings.

There is no application-wide task registry, so this capability has no single legacy owner. Task truth is split across protocol-specific controller Maps, child operations, component refs, hooks, and promises; those existing owners remain attributed to their protocol or application-workflow capabilities.
Current processing reports success with a raw outputPath before local-save or UploadManager delivery reaches a terminal state.

No staged-output lease owner exists in the legacy runtime. Raw paths and temporary directories are returned by protocol task functions and held by renderer workflows; there is no opaque lease, TTL, owner task, reaper, or quarantine.

HLS now recovers a bounded main-owned task projection after renderer listener remount, but processing and delivery are still not a single application-scoped workflow. In particular, the frozen library target and UploadManager handoff remain feature-scoped, so live recording must discard on tool unmount until this coordinator and staged-output lease exist.
UploadManager is the upload task owner, but the current embedded-browser workflow awaits creation flow rather than maintaining a durable processing/delivery association.
Seed only: filename filtering, template evaluation, large-buffer conversion, and direct data-URL output are anchored, but helper consumers and output semantics remain unmapped.

The current main-process file-save service copies or writes extracted resource bytes to a user-selected path, but delivery terminal state and staged-output release are not yet owned by the planned adapter.

Normal BrowserWindow download completion and optional library import form a separate OmniFlow handoff from captured-output local save and retain their own cleanup lifecycle. Cat Catch browser-download fallback and downloader-page lifecycle are mapped under the transfer capabilities instead of being conflated with this local contract.

Manifest download and manifest track merge now share a cancel-aware process runner: HLS calls register its AbortSignal with the tab/request owner, termination uses the cross-platform process-tree adapter, and aborted/non-zero tasks remove partial output. A conditional real-binary integration verifies the manifest runner produces a probeable MP4/AAC output from generated local HLS. Executable probing, resource merge, resource transcode, and MPD track merge remain separate child-process sites, so no application-wide ffmpeg task/app-exit owner exists yet.

Pinned upstream Base64-encodes m3u8dl custom-protocol payloads when configured. The unregistered ExternalToolDispatcher now accepts only tabId, opaque resourceId, and toolKey, redeems URL/metadata/protected headers from the main-owned Store/Vault, and rejects invalid, cross-tab, or stale requests before execution. Production IPC/preload/renderer still call the legacy generic protocol/command/aria2 dispatcher with renderer-supplied URL/header payloads; process terminal behavior, m3u8dl Base64 protocol encoding, production wiring, and legacy cleanup remain open. Options import/export is a separate peripheral Base64 consumer and remains outside this initial runtime mapping.
